result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_forest()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if the graph is a forest. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L6005-L6090){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_forest() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is forest](/assets/graphs/is-forest.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: two separate trees, one on A, B, D, E and one on C and F; neither has a cycle, so is_forest() returns True. Right: the same two trees plus an edge between D and E, which closes the triangle B, D, E (shown in the accent color), so is_forest() returns False." width="100%"} A forest is an acyclic, undirected graph (disjoint union of trees). For a graph with *n* nodes and *k* connected components to be a forest it: - must be undirected - must have exactly *n - k* edges - must be acyclic ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if graph is a forest, `False` otherwise. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A forest is exactly the disjoint union of trees, so a single tree is a forest with $k = 1$, and the empty graph is a forest with $k = 0$. The edge-count law $|E| = n - k$ drops straight out of applying $|E| = n_i - 1$ to each of the $k$ component trees and summing over $i$; combined with acyclicity this is what the check actually verifies. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A single tree already satisfies the forest definition, since a tree is just a forest with one component: ::: {#55ec8d80 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec tree = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") ) tree.is_forest() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Unlike `is_tree()`, this doesn't require a single connected component -- several disjoint trees together still form a forest: ::: {#c32b4dc2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} forest = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_edge("A", "B") # first tree .add_edge("C", "D") # second, disjoint tree ) forest.is_forest(), forest.is_tree() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: ::: A cycle breaks the "acyclic" requirement, so it's neither a forest nor a tree: ::: {#304552ef .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} cycle = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") .add_edge("C", "A") ) cycle.is_forest() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` False ``` ::: ::: An empty graph vacuously satisfies the definition too: ::: {#b4b60d31 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph(directed=False).is_forest() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: :::
